weeks.title: Intro to ML + Linear Regression
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · build the mental model first
weeks.mindset: Coming from engineering: a model is just a function with tunable constants. f(x) = wx + b is the whole hypothesis. "Training" is nothing more than a loop that nudges w and b downhill on an error surface. No magic — cost function, derivative, step, repeat.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain supervised vs unsupervised in one sentence each, write the squared-error cost by hand, and implement gradient descent for one variable in NumPy without looking it up.

tasks.content: Watch Week 1 — Overview of Machine Learning and "What is machine learning?". Write a one-line definition in your own words.
Watch Supervised learning part 1 & 2 and Unsupervised learning part 1 & 2.
List 3 problems from your own work and label each supervised / unsupervised, with the input x and target y named explicitly.
Watch Linear regression model part 1 & 2. Learn the notation: m examples, x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾, ŷ.
Watch Cost function formula and Cost function intuition.

Write J(w,b) from memory on paper. Check it against the lecture slide.
Complete the optional lab: Model representation.
Complete the optional lab: Cost function.
From a blank file, implement compute_cost(X, y, w, b) in NumPy. No loops — use vectorized operations.
Watch Gradient descent and Implementing gradient descent.
Watch Gradient descent intuition and Learning rate. Note what happens when α is too large vs too small.
Watch Gradient descent for linear regression and Running gradient descent.
Derive ∂J/∂w and ∂J/∂b by hand. This is the only derivation in the course you should be able to reproduce cold.
Complete the optional lab: Gradient descent.
Build a single-variable linear regression from scratch on a toy dataset — cost, gradients, and the descent loop, all your own code.
Plot cost vs iteration. If it is not monotonically decreasing, your gradient or learning rate is wrong — debug before moving on.
Take the Week 1 practice quizzes until you score 100%.
Explain gradient descent out loud in 60 seconds without notes.
Fill in the Retro Log: what clicked, what did not, what to revisit.

weeks.title: Multiple Features + Practical Gradient Descent
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · vectorization is the unlock
weeks.mindset: Vectorization is not an optimization, it is the language. Once f = np.dot(w, x) + b replaces the loop, the math and the code look the same. Every later topic — neural networks included — is written this way. Fight to make everything a matrix operation now.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can implement multiple linear regression fully vectorized, know when feature scaling is required, and can diagnose a bad learning rate from the cost curve alone.

tasks.content: Watch Multiple features and Vectorization part 1 & 2.
Watch Gradient descent for multiple linear regression.
Benchmark a Python loop vs np.dot on 100k elements. Record the speedup — this is why vectorization matters.
Complete the optional lab: Python, NumPy and vectorization.
Complete the optional lab: Multiple linear regression.
Rewrite last week's single-variable model to accept an (m, n) matrix X with zero Python loops in the gradient.
Watch Feature scaling part 1 & 2. Understand z-score normalization.
Watch Checking gradient descent for convergence and Choosing the learning rate.
Note the α sweep heuristic: try 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and compare cost curves.
Watch Feature engineering and Polynomial regression.
Complete the optional labs: Feature scaling and learning rate, Feature engineering and polynomial regression.
Complete the optional lab: Linear regression with scikit-learn. Compare its output to your own implementation.
Complete the graded lab: Linear Regression (Week 2 assignment).
Start Project 1 — House Price Predictor: load a real housing dataset, apply z-score scaling, fit multiple linear regression.
Report train MSE and compare against a baseline that always predicts the mean. Beat the baseline or find out why not.
Take the Week 2 practice quizzes until you score 100%.
Write down, from memory, why feature scaling speeds up gradient descent.
Fill in the Retro Log.

weeks.title: Logistic Regression + Regularization
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · classification and the overfitting problem
weeks.mindset: Do not reuse squared error for classification. It produces a non-convex surface full of local minima. Log loss exists specifically to restore a single global minimum. When a new cost function appears, ask what shape it makes — that is the whole reason it was chosen.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can implement logistic regression with regularization, explain the decision boundary geometrically, and describe three concrete fixes for overfitting.

tasks.content: Watch Motivations and Logistic regression. Understand why linear regression fails on classification.
Watch Decision boundary. Sketch the boundary for a 2-feature example by hand.
Complete the optional labs: Classification, Sigmoid function and logistic regression, Decision boundary.

Watch Gradient descent implementation for logistic regression.

Complete the optional labs: Logistic loss, Cost function for logistic regression, Gradient descent for logistic regression.
Implement sigmoid, compute_cost_logistic and compute_gradient_logistic from scratch.

Complete the graded lab: Logistic Regression (Week 3 assignment).

Fill in the Retro Log.

weeks.title: Neural Networks — Intuition & Forward Propagation
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · a layer is just many logistic units
weeks.mindset: A neural network is not a new idea, it is composition. One neuron is the logistic regression you already wrote. A layer is several of them sharing an input. A network is layers chained together. Nothing new is introduced this week except notation for stacking.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can hand-compute a forward pass through a 2-layer network, build the same network in TensorFlow, and implement forward prop in raw NumPy.

tasks.content: Watch Neurons and the brain and Demand prediction.

weeks.title: Training Neural Networks — Activations, Softmax, Adam
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · why non-linearity is mandatory
weeks.mindset: Stack linear layers and you still have a linear model. The activation function is the only reason depth buys anything. ReLU is the default not because it is elegant but because it does not saturate and it trains fast. Choose the output activation from the problem type, never by habit.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain the three steps of model training in TensorFlow, pick the right activation for any layer, and describe why softmax needs a numerically stable implementation.

weeks.title: Applying ML — Bias, Variance & Error Analysis
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · the most practically useful week
weeks.mindset: This is the week that separates people who ship models from people who tune randomly. Every wasted month in an ML project traces back to fixing variance when the problem was bias. Learn to read the train/CV gap before you touch a hyperparameter.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can diagnose bias vs variance from two numbers, know which fix each one calls for, and can run an error analysis that actually redirects your effort.

Watch Establishing a baseline level of performance and Learning curves.

weeks.title: Decision Trees & Ensembles
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · the algorithm that wins on tabular data
weeks.mindset: Neural networks are not the default answer. For structured, tabular data — most business problems — a gradient-boosted tree usually wins, trains in seconds, and is far easier to explain to a stakeholder. Knowing when not to reach for a neural network is a senior skill.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can compute entropy and information gain by hand, explain why random forests decorrelate trees, and state a clear rule for trees vs neural networks.

weeks.title: Clustering & Anomaly Detection
weeks.mindset: No labels means no accuracy score. You cannot validate these models the way you validated a classifier — you evaluate them by whether the structure they find is useful. K-means also has local minima, which is why you run it several times and keep the best cost. Random restarts are part of the algorithm, not a hack.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can implement K-means end to end, choose K defensibly, and explain when anomaly detection beats supervised classification.

weeks.title: Recommender Systems & PCA
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · learning features and parameters together
weeks.mindset: Collaborative filtering learns the features as well as the weights. That is the genuinely new idea this week — gradient descent optimizes x and w simultaneously. Content-based filtering is the opposite: features are given, and two networks learn to embed them into the same space.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain collaborative vs content-based filtering, know why mean normalization matters for new users, and can state what PCA actually preserves.

weeks.title: Reinforcement Learning + Capstone
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · reward instead of labels
weeks.mindset: RL replaces the label with a reward signal. You never tell the agent the right action — only how good the outcome was, often much later. The Bellman equation is just the recursive statement of that idea. Everything else this week is machinery for approximating Q(s,a) when the state space is continuous.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have finished the specialization: the lunar lander trains, all three projects are on GitHub, and you can explain the Bellman equation without notes.
